source: JZ Mock C · Paper 2 · Question 20 · Publisher worked answer
label: JZ Mock C · Paper 2 · Question 20
knowledgePattern: Prove a rhombus guarantee and construct convex counterexamples to weaker conditions
solution:
Test each condition separately. Let O be the intersection of the diagonals when considering the four small triangles.

For condition 2, adjacent angles at O are supplementary. If they were unequal, the common shape of all four similar triangles would have to contain both those supplementary angles, leaving no positive third angle. Therefore the diagonals are perpendicular.

Now triangles AOB and COD are similar right triangles with equal hypotenuses AB = CD, so they are congruent. Put OA = a, OB = b, OC = c, OD = d. Their unordered pairs of legs agree. If a = c and b = d, all four side lengths are equal by Pythagoras. If instead a = d and b = c, triangle BOC has equal legs. Since every small triangle is similar to it, all are right isosceles, again making all four sides equal. Thus condition 2 guarantees a rhombus, including the possible swapped correspondence.

Condition 1 fails for the convex kite A=(1,0),B=(0,1),C=(−2,0),D=(0,−1). Its diagonals are perpendicular and AB=AD=2, but BC=CD=5.

Condition 3 fails for the convex kite A=(9/5,12/5),B=(0,0),C=(9/5,−12/5),D=(5,0). The four small right triangles have legs 9/5 and 12/5, or 12/5 and 16/5, so all have the same 3:4:5 shape. Yet AB=BC=3 and CD=DA=4.

Condition 4 holds for any nonsquare rectangle: each diagonal divides its area equally, so all four large triangles have the same area. Its adjacent side lengths need not be equal.

Condition 5 fails for the convex trapezium A=(−1,0),B=(−1/2,3/2),C=(1/2,3/2),D=(1,0). Here AB=BC=CD=1, AC=BD=3, so ABC and BCD are congruent by SSS, but AD = 2.

Only condition 2 is sufficient. Answer B.

hints.title: Separate guarantees from examples
hints.body: For each listed condition, either show that all four sides must be equal or build a convex quadrilateral meeting that condition with unequal sides.
hints.recap: A sufficient condition must force the target in every allowed case; one allowed counterexample disproves sufficiency.
hints.pitfall: Each condition is considered by itself; do not carry assumptions from another condition.
hints.pause: Test familiar quadrilateral families, checking every stated equality rather than relying on appearance.

recall.reminder: A sufficient condition must force the target in every allowed case; one allowed counterexample disproves sufficiency.

hints.title: Exploit a common triangle shape
hints.body: When the diagonals form four similar triangles, compare their adjacent angles at the intersection using the straight-line angle sum.
hints.recap: Adjacent angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees, while a triangle has three positive angles summing to 180 degrees.
hints.pitfall: Similar triangles may use different correspondences: equal-looking positions are not automatically corresponding vertices.
hints.pause: Determine what the common shape forces at the diagonal intersection.

recall.reminder: Adjacent angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees, while a triangle has three positive angles summing to 180 degrees.

hints.title: Check whether equal length fixes the scale
hints.body: Once the small-triangle shapes are known, examine how a stated equal side pair restricts their scale. Include every possible correspondence of the other sides.
hints.recap: Similar triangles share one positive scale factor across corresponding lengths; a matched equal side fixes that factor.
hints.pitfall: A proof that overlooks a swapped side correspondence is incomplete.
hints.pause: Use these facts to decide which listed conditions force all four sides equal; prove each accepted one and check any counterexamples for the others.

recall.reminder: Similar triangles share one positive scale factor across corresponding lengths; a matched equal side fixes that factor.
